1.pericope_label: Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God. Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem, and cry unto her, that her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned: for she hath received of the Lord’s hand double for all her sins.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch answer the question of where this begins with architecture, the second half of the book falling into three parts of three times three addresses; Ellicott works the double as a campaign finished and a debt discharged, hears in my people an echo of the earlier prophet, and notes the address formula as peculiar to this book and common to both halves.

Gill marks the turn from the captivity predicted before into the more evangelical part of the prophecy and takes Jerusalem for the Gospel church; Calvin reconstructs the occasion, a prophet making no impression on his generation turning to posterity, and reads speaking to the heart as speaking according to its wish.

Clarke refuses the plain sense of the double as irreconcilable with a justice that always punishes less than iniquity deserves, and adds words to his version to get blessings double to the punishment; Wesley takes the middle, enough to answer the design of the chastisement.

Henry widens the charge to comfort in three steps, warranting the prophet for his own day, directing those who would live through the captivity, and putting gospel ministers in mind of their business.

debates.question: What is the double she has received at the LORD's hand?

positions.position: Affliction ended, debt paid, double received from the LORD's hand.
A campaign finished and a debt strictly paid off, the exile one long war with enemies worse than the conquerors.
Not double punishment, which divine justice forbids, but blessings double to the punishment.
Not twice what her sins deserved, but enough to answer the design of the chastisement.

debates.question: Who is the Jerusalem addressed?

positions.position: The Gospel church, with the Jewish reading making her the congregation of Israel.
The holy city itself, thought of with the people belonging to it.

debates.question: Who is charged to comfort?

positions.position: Prophets and ministers.
The prophet for his own day, the prophets of the captivity, and gospel ministers alike.
Prophets foreseen working towards the close of the exile.
Not so much the prophets exhorted to courage as believers given an assured hope to bear the delay.

outliers.claim: Opens on authorship with a declared assumption rather than an argument, that the poem which follows is the prophet's own, and refers the question elsewhere.
Reports besides the Jewish reading that the double is the two captivities, the Babylonian and the one still endured.

themes: Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God.
Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem, and cry unto her, that her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned: for she hath received of the Lord’s hand double for all her sins.

3.pericope_label: The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make straight in the desert a highway for our God. Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low: and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain: and the glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together: for the mouth of the Lord hath spoken it.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch put the wilderness with the command rather than the crier and keep the summons in a commanding tone; Ellicott requires the same punctuation from parallelism, reaches for the road-making of eastern kings boasted of in the Assyrian inscriptions, and gives four levellings in a line as the true work of every follower of the Baptist.

Gill keeps the English attachment of the wilderness, rejects the Jewish reading that makes the crier the Holy Ghost, and takes the levelling parabolically of the guilty raised and the self-righteous brought low; Calvin takes the wilderness metaphorically of the desolation then existing and keeps the passage on the Church's deliverance.

Clarke repunctuates with the others, describes the harbingers and pioneers of eastern monarchs, doubts the usual rendering of crooked, and argues that the Greek addition of the salvation of our God is genuine; Wesley reads the same royal custom off as God disposing hearts and ordering affairs to make way.
Henry allows the prophets among the captives first and then insists on the Baptist.

debates.question: Where does the wilderness belong in the sentence?

positions.position: With the command and not the crier: a voice of one crying, In the wilderness prepare ye.
With the crier, the crying located in the wilderness.
Metaphorically, of the desolation then existing, without denying the road between Judea and Babylon.

debates.question: Who is the crier?

positions.position: The Baptist, and a teaching voice rather than a mere sound.
Deliberately unnamed, the herald content to efface himself and be a voice or nothing.
The prophets among the captives first, and then the Baptist.
Immediately the return from Babylon, principally the Messiah.

debates.question: Is the levelling commanded or foretold?

positions.position: Commanded: let every valley be exalted, let the rugged be made a plain.
Properly imperative, with others taking the command as running on from the opening.
Future.

outliers.claim: Argues a textual case for the Greek addition of the salvation of our God: the sentence is abrupt without it since the verb wants its object, and the words stand in every Greek copy and are acknowledged in the gospel.

Leaves the glory an open question, whether the prophet thought of a glory-cloud like the one seen in the temple or had risen to a glory of character and will, and marks all flesh, meeting us here first, as the growing catholicity of his thought.

themes: The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make straight in the desert a highway for our God.
Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low: and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain:
And the glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together: for the mouth of the Lord hath spoken it.

6.pericope_label: The voice said, Cry. And he said, What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field: the grass withereth, the flower fadeth: because the spirit of the Lord bloweth upon it: surely the people is grass. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch hear a second and then a third voice in conversation and put the contrast of withering grass and abiding word as the point of the exchange; Ellicott argues the wind of Jehovah as a destructive storm-blast from within the parable, and frames the fading flower both literarily, beside the line on the generations of leaves, and biographically, as the natural sentiment of a man in extreme old age.

Gill sets aside the Jewish readings that make the voice an angel or prophecy and takes it for the Lord's own commission, without which none may preach lawfully, and reads the repeated withering as raising attention; Calvin marks the change of speaker as fixing when the Lord commands and when his ministers execute, and gives the repetition a double office of humbling and consoling.

Clarke calls a wind of Jehovah a plain Hebraism for a strong wind, notes the hot east wind that destroys every green thing, and reports manuscript evidence against the divine name and against the verse itself; Wesley draws the practical conclusion, that the word is like God himself, immutable and irresistible.

debates.question: What is the wind that blows on the grass?

positions.position: A plain Hebraism for a strong wind, the hot east wind that destroys every green thing.
A storm-blast tearing the grass up, since the agency inside the parable is destructive rather than quickening.
Allowable, but better taken as the metaphor fitted to the subject: men with all their gifts carried off by one breath of the Spirit.

debates.question: Who is the second voice, and who answers it?

positions.position: The Lord's own voice to the prophet, or rather to any gospel minister.
God commanding the prophets, distinct from the prophets' own voice earlier.
A second and then a third voice in conversation, the second appointing a preacher of the promise's endurance.
The prophet himself is the questioner.

debates.question: How wide is the word that stands for ever?

positions.position: Primarily the prophetic word revealing God's will, but taking in every manifestation of his being.
The word like God himself, immutable and irresistible, so that fulfilment is past doubting.
The abiding term of the contrast: grass withers and flower fades, yet the word of our God will stand for ever.

outliers.claim: Reports that the whole verse may not belong here, being wanting in three manuscripts of one collator and five of another, in an ancient copy of his own, and in the Greek and the Arabic.

Offers the fading flower as biographical evidence: a man in extreme old age, looking back over the generations he had outlived and forward to the fall of one great monarchy after another, would think in these terms.

themes: The voice said, Cry. And he said, What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field:
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: because the spirit of the Lord bloweth upon it: surely the people is grass.
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.

9.pericope_label: O Zion, that bringest good tidings, get thee up into the high mountain; lift up thy voice with strength; be not afraid; say unto the cities of Judah, Behold your God! Behold, the Lord God will come with strong hand, and his arm shall rule for him: behold, his reward is with him, and his work before him. He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch refuse the rendering with strength and take the particle as one of essence, and mark the shepherd as the turn from the judicial side to the redeeming; Ellicott reads the coming the same way, notes the arm as a favourite word and the doubled divine name as characteristic of both halves, and stops with feeling over the first occurrence of the word for good tidings.

Gill prefers the reading that makes Zion the recipient, hears the second coming in the reward, and fills in whose flock it is, one flock, little, and often a flock of slaughter; Calvin has the message given first to Zion and then spread through the other cities, reports a third construction of the coming, and explains why an image was needed at all.

Clarke argues at length that the true construction makes Zion the receiver, grounds the feminine in the custom by which women announced a signal victory, and reads the nursing ewes gently led from a patriarch's plea and a traveller's account; Wesley makes Zion the publisher and will not have the recompense one-sided, blessing for friends and vengeance for enemies.
Henry keeps both sides of the quarrel, notice given to the remnant in Zion and to the captives who belonged to her.

debates.question: Does Zion carry the news or receive it?

positions.position: Receives it, as agreeing better with the rest of the verse.
Receives it: the publisher reading has prevailed, but the true construction makes her the receiver, and the feminine needs the word daughter in English.
Carries it: the participle is feminine, and no female herald but Jerusalem has appeared.
Carries it, Zion the publisher and the cities of Judah the hearers.
Given first to Zion and now spread through the other cities.
Both, notice given to the remnant in Zion and to the captives belonging to her.

debates.question: How does the LORD come with a strong hand?

positions.position: Not with strength, as the Greek and the Targum give, but in the energy of a strong one, his arm ruling for him.
A third construction has stood in respectable company: against the strong one, against the nations, to punish them.

debates.question: What is the reward he brings before him?

positions.position: What God bestows and will pay to his faithful servants, held out in front to encourage those who wait.
Recompenses both ways, blessing for his friends and vengeance for his enemies.
The second coming, when the reward is given to every man according to his works.

outliers.claim: Stops over the first occurrence of the term which, passing through the Greek into the later scriptures, became the word carrying the message of good tidings to mankind.
Grounds the feminine participle in a custom: announcing and celebrating a great public success or a signal victory belonged peculiarly to the women.

themes: O Zion, that bringest good tidings, get thee up into the high mountain; O Jerusalem, that bringest good tidings, lift up thy voice with strength; lift it up, be not afraid; say unto the cities of Judah, Behold your God!
Behold, the Lord God will come with strong hand, and his arm shall rule for him: behold, his reward is with him, and his work before him.
He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young.

12.pericope_label: Who hath measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and meted out heaven with the span, and comprehended the dust of the earth in a measure? Who hath directed the Spirit of the Lord, or being his counsellor hath taught him? With whom took he counsel, and who instructed him, and taught him in the path of judgment? Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance. All nations before him are as nothing; and they are counted to him less than nothing, and vanity.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch keep the questions on Jehovah, the first recalling his omnipotence and the second his omniscience, and mark the word that means what suffices rather than what is required; Ellicott holds the Spirit here clothed with a divine personality answering to the figure of wisdom, sets the passage against an eastern cosmogony, and keeps finding the neighbourhood of the wisdom books.

Gill takes the whole account of power and wisdom to be Christ's, given to show him equal to the redemption he has undertaken, and puts the nations as nonentity beside the Being of beings; Calvin defends the crowded manner as fitted to its object, a support of faith, and raises the objection about the nations himself before answering it by comparison.

Clarke alone turns the insufficiency of the forest toward atonement, asking whether all the offerings that could be made were insufficient to atone for sin; Wesley keeps to the figures, the dust cleaving to the balance without altering the weight and the isles that are the countries reached from Judea by sea.

Henry gives three reasons for the description of greatness here: to encourage captives to depend on him though weak, to hold them from other gods since none compare, and to fill those who receive the glad tidings with awe.

debates.question: Whose greatness is being described?

positions.position: Christ's, given to show him equal to the redemption he has undertaken, so that it is his Spirit whom none counselled in creation.
Jehovah's, the questions recalling his omnipotence and his omniscience.

debates.question: What does the insufficiency of Lebanon prove?

positions.position: That the whole forest could not afford a sacrifice answerable to what God deserves, Lebanon being the type of the forests that supplied wood for burnt offerings.
That all the offerings that could be made were insufficient to atone for sin, and therefore the Redeemer was to come.

debates.question: What is the Spirit of the second question?

positions.position: The Spirit that moved on the waters at creation, with none beside him to advise.
The word clothed here with a divine personality, answering to the figure of wisdom.
A rebuke to carnal sense, which limits God's power to human means and doubts whatever it cannot see the way to.

outliers.claim: Sets the passage against an eastern cosmogony whose chief god might call lesser deities into counsel, where this prophet finds no counsellor but one essentially one with the Eternal.

Raises the objection to calling the nations nothing himself, since God created them that they might be something, and answers that it is said by comparison, so that whatever is compared with God is worthless.

themes: Who hath measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and meted out heaven with the span, and comprehended the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighed the mountains in scales, and the hills in a balance?
Who hath directed the Spirit of the Lord, or being his counsellor hath taught him?
With whom took he counsel, and who instructed him, and taught him in the path of judgment, and taught him knowledge, and shewed to him the way of understanding?
Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance: behold, he taketh up the isles as a very little thing.
And Lebanon is not sufficient to burn, nor the beasts thereof sufficient for a burnt offering.
All nations before him are as nothing; and they are counted to him less than nothing, and vanity.

18.pericope_label: To whom then will ye liken God? or what likeness will ye compare unto him? The workman melteth a graven image, and the goldsmith spreadeth it over with gold. Have ye not known? have ye not heard? hath it not been told you from the beginning? It is he that sitteth upon the circle of the earth, and the inhabitants thereof are as grasshoppers; that bringeth the princes to nothing; he maketh the judges of the earth as vanity. To whom then will ye liken me, or shall I be equal? saith the Holy One. Lift up your eyes on high, and behold who hath created these things.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch address the challenge not to idolaters but to Israelites needing arming, describe the plating and the melted silver chains, and place the circle overhead as the vault arching over the earth; Ellicott marks the prophet's sarcasm against the apostle's pity at Athens, infers from the idol shop that the reigns the prophet lived through supplied the picture, and reads the marshalling of the host as an expansion of the divine name of hosts.

Gill calls the passage an antidote against idolatry in Babylon, reports two constructions of the poor man's offering, and takes the circle of the globe itself, hung as a ball in the air; Calvin has the prophet turn from the Gentiles to his own people, diagnoses idolatry as arising from the wish to enjoy God's presence, and admits the prophet seems to linger on what nobody disputes.

Clarke draws the moral of gold for the rich and wood for the poor, quotes a traveller's awning spread on ropes across a court for the curtain, and passes on a rabbinic saying that a man capable of meditating on the heavenly bodies and not doing it is unworthy to be named among men; Wesley reads the immovable image as impotent and keeps the earth itself round.
Henry sorts the folly in two, representing God by creatures and putting creatures in his place.

debates.question: What is the circle over which God sits?

positions.position: The globe of the earth itself, hung as a ball in the air rather than a flat plain.
The vault of heaven arching over the earth.

debates.question: What does the immovable idol show?

positions.position: Stability sought at the cheap extreme of idolatry, a useless log standing on its own wide base.
Impotence: an image that cannot stir a step to help you.

debates.question: Who is the challenge aimed at?

positions.position: Israelites needing arming against a seduction most of mankind had yielded to.
An antidote against their falling into idolatry in Babylon.
The prophet's own people, turning from the Gentiles.
The primary intuitions of mankind rather than the commandments of the law.

outliers.claim: Traces idolatry to a right wish gone wrong: men desire to enjoy the presence of God, and that desire is the beginning and source of idolatry, since God is present by his word and Spirit and not by an idol.
Draws a conclusion about the writer from the idol shop, that the reigns the prophet had lived through must have supplied the picture as fully as living in Babylon would have done.

themes: To whom then will ye liken God? or what likeness will ye compare unto him?
The workman melteth a graven image, and the goldsmith spreadeth it over with gold, and casteth silver chains.
He that is so impoverished that he hath no oblation chooseth a tree that will not rot; he seeketh unto him a cunning workman to prepare a graven image, that shall not be moved.
Have ye not known? have ye not heard? hath it not been told you from the beginning? have ye not understood from the foundations of the earth?
It is he that sitteth upon the circle of the earth, and the inhabitants thereof are as grasshoppers; that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in:
That bringeth the princes to nothing; he maketh the judges of the earth as vanity.

Yea, they shall not be planted; yea, they shall not be sown: yea, their stock shall not take root in the earth: and he shall also blow upon them, and they shall wither, and the whirlwind shall take them away as stubble.
To whom then will ye liken me, or shall I be equal? saith the Holy One.

Lift up your eyes on high, and behold who hath created these things, that bringeth out their host by number: he calleth them all by names by the greatness of his might, for that he is strong in power; not one faileth.

27.pericope_label: Why sayest thou, O Jacob, and speakest, O Israel, My way is hid from the Lord, and my judgment is passed over from my God? Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the Lord, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength. Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall: but they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch address the complaint to the despondent who still desire salvation, gloss the way as their thorny way of life and the right as their good right against oppressors, and reduce the requirement to faith alone; Ellicott makes the eternity a ground of comfort and not only a rebuke, asks whether the prophet had come to feel his own earlier anthropomorphism misleading, and traces the unsearchable understanding to the book of Job.

Gill takes the complainers for the captives of the older commentators or the church under Rome pagan or papal, lists where they might have learned better, and spends himself on what waiting is; Calvin allows such murmurs were probably heard, argues from the word eternal that what is eternal never changes or decays, and makes waiting mean patience against the violent who dash themselves to pieces.

Clarke keeps to the text on the conjunction and reports at length the old belief that the eagle moults in age and renews its youth, declining to adjudicate it; Wesley puts the grievance plainly and takes the failing youths as the youngest and strongest, left to themselves.
Henry makes the doubling of saying and speaking the fault, divides the despair into God not heeding and God not helping, and turns the failing youths inward, to those who trust their own sufficiency.

debates.question: Who are the youths that faint and fall?

positions.position: Men in the prime of strength who glory in it, and, with the Targum and the Jewish commentators, the wicked, applied to the emperors who persecuted the church and the antichristian states.
Those who trust their own sufficiency and so neither exert themselves to the utmost nor seek grace.
The youngest and strongest, left to themselves.
The age when vigour is at its highest, the second word a nearer approach to manhood.

debates.question: What answers the complaint that God has overlooked them?

positions.position: The names themselves, recalling an ancestor who found God faithful in all his straits.
The same names, as recalling the covenant ratified by promises.
The eternity of God, no transient favour and no capricious will.
That the Creator of the ends of the earth had Babylon well within the range of his vision and power.

debates.question: What is it to renew strength?

positions.position: The Hebrew idiom of exchanging strength, and a waiting that means patience.
Putting forth fresh feathers like the moulting eagle.
Lifting up their wings, on the same belief about the plumage.

outliers.claim: Declines to adjudicate the eagle legend at all: it is enough for a poet, profane or sacred, to have popular opinion behind an image introduced for illustration or ornament.
Turns waiting into a set of postures: children on parents, servants on masters, clients on patrons, and beggars who knock, meet repulses, and keep their place.

themes: Why sayest thou, O Jacob, and speakest, O Israel, My way is hid from the Lord, and my judgment is passed over from my God?
Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the Lord, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? there is no searching of his understanding.
He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength.
Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall:
But they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
